propositions.text: The claimant is a Turkish citizen seeking refugee protection under IRPA subsections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: The claimant, XXXXXXX, is a citizen of Turkey who seeks refugee protection pursuant to subsections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is a Turkish citizen seeking refugee protection under IRPA subsections 96 and 97(1), court states.

propositions.text: The claimant fears returning to Turkey due to involvement with Alevi-Kurdish leftist activities and past detentions and torture.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he fears returning to Turkey due to his involvement with Alevi-Kurdish leftist activities where he was detained, beaten and tortured four separate times.

propositions.text: The claimant objects to serving in the Turkish military due to expected human rights violations against Kurds.
propositions.quote: The claimant also objects in serving in the Turkish military due to the human rights violations of the military that he believes he will be required to commit against Kurds like himself.

propositions.text: The claimant left Turkey in 2008, arrived illegally in Canada in 2010, and filed a refugee claim on November 15, 2010.
propositions.quote: The claimant departed Turkey on XXXX, 2008 for the United States and arrived illegally in Canada at Vancouver on XXXXXXX, 2010 and filed a refugee claim on November 15, 2010.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges fear of return due to past torture and military objections, left Turkey in 2008, arrived in Canada in 2010, filed claim November 2010, claimant states.

propositions.text: The panel finds the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The panel finds no personal risk of life or cruel treatment if claimant returns to Turkey.
propositions.quote: The panel also finds that should the claimant return to Turkey he would not be subjected personally to a risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

propositions.text: There are no substantial grounds to believe the claimant faces danger of torture if returned.
propositions.quote: Further, on substantial grounds there is no danger of torture.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant is not a refugee or protected person and faces no personal risk of harm or torture if returned, court finds.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, the panel accepts claimant's Turkish citizenship based on passport copies.
propositions.quote: On a balance of probabilities, the panel is willing to accept that the claimant is a citizen of Turkey based on copies of his passport as seen in exhibit R/A-2.

paragraphs.summary: The panel accepts claimant's Turkish citizenship based on passport copies, court finds.

propositions.text: The key issue is the credibility of the claimant's evidence.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this case is the credibility of the evidence as submitted.

propositions.text: Sellan case states lack of credibility finding disposes claim unless independent credible evidence supports it; claimant bears onus.
propositions.quote: On the issue of credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal case in Sellan3 which stated the following: Where the Board makes a general finding that the claimant lacks credibility, that determination is sufficient to dispose of the claim unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence in the record capable of supporting a positive disposition of the claim. The claimant bears the onus of demonstrating there was such evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The key issue is claimant's credibility; Sellan requires independent credible evidence if credibility is lacking, court states.

propositions.text: Federal Court says Board is better placed to assess credibility; findings only overturned if perverse or ignoring material.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Federal Court notes the following: The Board is in a much better position than a reviewing court to gage the credibility and plausibility of a refugee claimant's story. A credibility finding is not a finding of mixed fact and law. It is a finding of fact, pure and simple. Findings of fact made by the Board may only be interfered with by a reviewing court if the finding was made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard for the material before it (see the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, paragraph 18.1(4)(d)). Indeed, it was Parliament's express intention that administrative fact finding would command this high degree of deference (see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] S.C.J. No. 12 (QL) at paragraph 46). Thus, credibility findings of the Board are to be reviewed against the statutory standard of review provided for in paragraph 18.1(4)(d) of the Federal Courts Act (see Diabo v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1772, [2004] F.C.J. No. 2168 (QL) at paragraph 3).

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court says Board is better placed to assess credibility; findings only overturned if perverse or ignoring material, court states.

propositions.text: Claimant said he was involved with SIVAS, SDP, and Alevi groups supporting Kurdish human rights and was detained and tortured four times.
propositions.quote: The panel noted that the claimant's alleged activities with a human rights group, SIVAS, and his membership with SDP and Alevi associations was because he believed in the cause for Kurds and seeking their human rights. The claimant stated that the SDP and Alevi associations were aware of his activities which resulted in him being detained, beaten and tortured by the authorities in four separate occasions.

propositions.text: Claimant had no corroborating evidence from these groups to support his allegations.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked if he had any corroborating evidence from the alleged groups he was somehow involved with which could possibly credibly support his problems; he responded in the negative.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant said he was involved with Kurdish human rights groups and tortured four times but had no corroborating evidence, court notes.

propositions.text: There is a letter from a cultural association confirming claimant's membership from 2005 to 2010.
propositions.quote: The panel does recognize there is a brief letter from XXXXXXXXXX Cultural Association, as seen in Exhibit C-9, indicating the claimant's membership from the years 2005 to 2010.

propositions.text: The letter does not detail claimant's level of activities or problems with authorities.
propositions.quote: However, the letter provides no information as to the level of the claimant's activities and problems as alleged by the claimant from the authorities.

propositions.text: It is not unreasonable to expect claimant to provide corroborating evidence from groups aware of his problems.
propositions.quote: The panel does not find it would be such an unreasonable expectation for the claimant to have provided satisfactory corroborating evidence from the SDP or Alevi groups in Turkey that the claimant alleges membership or affiliation with regarding his problems from the authorities, given they were aware of his problems from the authorities.

propositions.text: Panel makes negative credibility finding due to lack of corroborating evidence about claimant's problems in Turkey.
propositions.quote: The panel makes a negative credibility finding for the lack of corroborating evidence pertaining to his alleged problems in Turkey.

paragraphs.summary: Panel notes letter confirming membership but no details; expects corroboration; finds claimant not credible for lack of evidence, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted an affidavit from his cousin attesting to claimant's activities and problems with authorities.
propositions.quote: The panel does recognize that in support of the claimant's problems, he submitted an Affidavit from his cousin, which was sworn on XXXXX, 2012. The Affidavit was submitted to attest to the claimant's activities and problems from authorities.

propositions.text: Panel gives little weight to cousin's affidavit as information is second hand and cousin was not in Turkey during alleged events.
propositions.quote: The panel gives little weight to the Affidavit from the claimant's cousin as the information obtained pertaining to the claimant's alleged situation in Turkey is second hand. The deponent, the claimant's cousin, was not in Turkey when the alleged problems of the claimant occurred.

propositions.text: Cousin obtained information from claimant's mother but no supporting evidence from her was provided.
propositions.quote: The deponent left Turkey in 1995 for the United States and came to Canada in XXXXX 2008. Therefore, the information by the deponent was obtained from the claimant's mother with no supporting evidence from the claimant's mother.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant submitted cousin's affidavit supporting activities, but panel gives little weight due to second-hand info and no supporting evidence, court finds.

propositions.text: No explanation why claimant's mother did not submit a letter detailing claimant's problems despite cousin's evidence from her.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, if the claimant did have problems from the authorities as alleged and for whatever reason he could not have obtained documentation from SIVAS, SDP or Alevi groups, then there is no indication why the claimant's mother did not submit a letter detailing the claimant's problems as alleged in Turkey for the panel to review and comment, given the claimant's cousin obtained evidence from the claimant's mother pertaining to his problems in Turkey.

propositions.text: Claimant bears burden to prove well-founded fear of persecution if returned to Turkey.
propositions.quote: The claimant has the burden of proving that he has a well founded fear of persecution if required to return to Turkey.

propositions.text: Lack of independent corroborating evidence negatively impacts claimant's credibility.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the lack of independent corroborating evidence also negatively impacts the credibility of the story as so alleged.

paragraphs.summary: Panel notes no letter from claimant's mother despite cousin's info; claimant bears burden; lack of corroboration harms credibility, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant attempted to provide corroborative evidence but documents lack independent credible info supporting political profile or risk to life.
propositions.quote: The panel acknowledges that the claimant has attempted to provide corroborative evidence to support his claim. However, the documents submitted inspires little confidence and lacks independent, credible information that would lead this panel to conclude that the claimant's political profile is what he wants this panel to believe and that as a consequence his life would be at risk.

propositions.text: Panel concerned about lack of corroboration from groups claimant allegedly affiliated with in Turkey.
propositions.quote: Also, the panel is duly concerned as to the lack of corroborating evidence from the groups and associations in Turkey the claimant was allegedly affiliated with as a member or otherwise.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimant's corroborative evidence unconvincing and lacks credible info; concerned about no corroboration from affiliated groups, court finds.

propositions.text: Panel rejects claimant's claim that organizations would be in trouble if they described his problems and sent evidence.
propositions.quote: The panel rejects the evidence from the claimant that the organizations would get into trouble if they describe his problems and send to the claimant.

propositions.text: Panel has insufficient evidence to conclude authorities would intercept evidence causing problems for associations.
propositions.quote: The panel has insufficient evidence to conclude that the authorities would intercept evidence submitted on behalf of the claimant which would in turn create problems for the association the claimant was allegedly involved with.

propositions.text: Claimant is not high profile enough to attract scrutiny from authorities, affecting believability negatively.
propositions.quote: The claimant is not a person of high profile or the like to create such scrutiny and interest from the authorities. This does negatively affect the believability of the story as put forward.

paragraphs.summary: Panel rejects claimant's claim that organizations risk trouble sending evidence; claimant not high profile; believability affected, court finds.

propositions.text: Credibility is a serious issue for the panel regarding the claim.
propositions.quote: Credibility is a serious issue for the panel regarding the claim as put forward.

propositions.text: Bhagat case states corroborating evidence not always necessary but absence can permit negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: On the issue of corroborating evidence, the panel wishes to note the following Federal Court case in Bhagat,4 which states the following: Corroborating evidence is not always necessary to establish the applicant's subjective fear. The Board, however, determined that in the particular circumstances of this case, corroborating evidence of persecution was expected. An absence of corroborating evidence, then, permitted it to make a negative inference against credibility of the applicant.

propositions.text: Sheik case says lack of credible evidence beyond applicant's testimony supports negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The respondent relies on Sheik v. Canada (M.E.I.) (C.A.), [1990] 3 F.C. 238, at page 244, for its argument that the Board did not err in law when making that conclusion: The concept of "credible evidence" is not, of course, the same as that of the credibility of the applicant, but it is obvious that where the only evidence before a tribunal linking the applicant to his claim is that of the applicant himself (in addition, perhaps, to "country reports" from which nothing about the applicant's claim can be directly deduced), a tribunal's perception that he is not a credible witness effectively amounts to a finding that there is no credible evidence on which the second-level tribunal could allow his claim.

propositions.text: Adu case states claimant's sworn testimony presumption is rebuttable by failure of expected documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: In Adu v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1995] F.C.J. No. 114 (QL), the Federal Court of Appeal found that it is reasonable to expect documentary evidence of the existence of a law and stated: The "presumption" that a claimant's sworn testimony is true is always rebuttable, and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention.

paragraphs.summary: Credibility is a serious issue; Federal Court cases Bhagat, Sheik, Adu support negative credibility in absence of corroboration, court notes.

propositions.text: Panel accepts claimant is Alevi and Kurd but not that his life is at risk as such.
propositions.quote: On a balance of probabilities, the panel is willing to accept that the claimant is an Alevi and Kurd but not that his life is at risk as an Alevi-Kurd, even though the panel recognizes that Alevis and Kurds, in reviewing the exhibits from counsel and the Board have and continue to experience problems in Turkey that are discriminatory and at times persecutory.

paragraphs.summary: Panel accepts claimant is Alevi and Kurd but not at risk of life as such, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant was not schooled in Kurdish school nor subjected to inferior education; has 14 years education and was employed 2006-2008.
propositions.quote: In this case as submitted, the claimant was not schooled at a school for Kurdish students nor was he subjected to inferior education due to being Kurdish. The claimant has 14 years of education and was a XXXXXXXXX from 2006 to 2008 in Turkey.

propositions.text: Credibility concerns and facts do not convince panel claimant suffered or would suffer persecution as Alevi-Kurd.
propositions.quote: Coupled with the credibility concerns as to the believability of the claimant's story, the panel has not been remotely convinced that as an Alevi-Kurd, the claimant suffered persecution as alleged or would suffer such persecution in the future if required to return to Turkey.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant had normal education and employment; panel not convinced he suffered or would suffer persecution as Alevi-Kurd, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant objects to military service fearing punishment for refusal and forced human rights abuses against Kurds.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the claimant also states he cannot return to Turkey as he objects to serving in the military and due to his objection he will be punished for refusing to serve. The claimant would need to know, if required to serve in the Turkish military, who he would be fighting with. If it is Kurds like him, he would be forced to commit human rights abuses and shoot his own people.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant objects to military service fearing punishment and forced abuses against Kurds, claimant argues.

propositions.text: Exhibit C-9 military document dated May 7, 2008 states claimant has no objection to service until Feb 21, 2011.
propositions.quote: In examining the evidence further, the panel wishes to note Exhibit C-9, pages 7-8, which is a military document issued at the request of the claimant dated May 7, 2008. The document states "the person whose identity information is stated below does not have any objection until 21.02.2011."

propositions.text: Panel doubts veracity of claimant's conscientious objection given he sought a letter indicating no objection until later date.
propositions.quote: If the claimant is a conscientious objector as he says he is, there is no credible reason why the claimant would have sought a military letter that indicates he has no objection until a later date. The panel does doubt the veracity of the evidence in relation to the claimant's alleged conscientious objection.

paragraphs.summary: Panel notes military document showing no objection until 2011 and doubts claimant's conscientious objection claim, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant said willingness to fight depends on situation; did not say he would never bear arms as conscientious objector.
propositions.quote: The panel asked the claimant whether he would join the military and fight if Turkey was invaded by a foreign nation. The claimant stated that it depends on the situation at the time and it would depend on why the foreign nation is invading Turkey. It is noted that the claimant did not say under any circumstances that he would not bear arms as a conscientious objector.

propositions.text: Conscientious objection alone does not amount to persecution where no alternative service exists; refusal punished by criminal prosecution as general law.
propositions.quote: However, even if the claimant had and he is truly a conscientious objector, that in of itself does not amount to persecution where a country does not have alternative service. In Turkey, as so seen in Exhibit C-5, if one refuses to serve in the military by reason of conscience, the punishment is criminal prosecution. This is a law of general application.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's willingness to fight depends on situation; conscientious objection alone is not persecution where refusal is criminal law, court states.

propositions.text: Hinzman and Ates cases hold repeated prosecution of conscientious objectors does not amount to persecution on Convention grounds.
propositions.quote: In Hinzman,5 the Federal Court stated the following: My conclusion in this regard is reinforced by the recent decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Ates v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2005] F.C.J. No. 1661. In Ates, the Court stated that even in a country where military service is compulsory and where there is no alternative to military service available, the repeated prosecutions and imprisonments of a sincere conscientious objector does not amount to persecution on a Convention ground. If persecution does not arise in the circumstances described in Ates, then surely the prosecution and potential imprisonment of a volunteer soldier by a country that does provide some, albeit limited, alternatives to military service would similarly not amount to persecution on a Convention ground.

paragraphs.summary: Hinzman and Ates cases hold prosecution of conscientious objectors is not persecution under Convention, court cites.

propositions.text: Claimant did not make asylum claim in US despite two and a half years there; passport confirms student visa valid 2008-2013.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the panel asked the claimant whether he made an asylum claim in the United States while in that country for two years and six months given the problems as alleged in his Personal Information Form and oral evidence. The claimant indicated that he entered the United States as a student in XXXXX and XXXXXXXX and that he did not make an asylum claim in the United States. The claimant's passport does confirm a five years multiple Visa issued on XXXX, 2008 and valid until XXXXX, 2013 for the purposes of study at XXXXX College in XXXXXX, Pennsylvania.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant did not seek asylum in US despite long stay; passport confirms valid student visa, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant was charged with several offenses in the US and convicted of disorderly conduct in 2009.
propositions.quote: he was charged with driving without a license, simple assault, reckless endangerment and two counts of disorderly conduct. The claimant was convicted on XXXXXX, 2009 of disorderly conduct.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the claimant's 2009 US conviction for disorderly conduct among other charges.

propositions.text: Claimant did not plan to claim asylum in the US due to US-Turkey alliance and intended to study and apply for US permanent residence.
propositions.quote: he did not plan on claiming in the United States as he heard he could not, or it would be difficult, as the United States and Turkey are allies. The claimant also says that it was his plan to finish his studies in the United States, apply for an employment authorization, and then apply for permanent residence in the U.S.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says he did not plan to claim asylum in the US and intended to study and seek permanent residence there.

propositions.text: Claimant subjectively did not consider claiming asylum in the US despite alleged mistreatment in Turkey, indicating lack of subjective and objective fear.
propositions.quote: it was not even a mere consideration for the claimant to claim asylum in the United States given his alleged problems...suggests clearly enough to the panel that the claimant never had it in his mind to seek asylum in the United States

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant did not consider US asylum, indicating lack of subjective and objective fear.

propositions.text: Court does not believe claimant's evidence that his US lawyer advised against asylum claim due to logic.
propositions.quote: The panel does not believe the claimant's evidence in this regard.

propositions.text: It makes little sense that lawyer would say asylum claim illogical if claimant wished to claim asylum after US criminal problems.
propositions.quote: If the claimant stated that he wished to claim asylum, after his criminal problems in the U.S., it makes little sense why his lawyer would say it is not logical

paragraphs.summary: The court disbelieves claimant's claim that his US lawyer advised against asylum claim as illogical.

propositions.text: Even if lawyer advised against asylum claim, claimant had no subjective or objective fear initially.
propositions.quote: even if his U.S. lawyer did state to the claimant that it was not a logical idea to claim asylum in the U.S., the fact is, as the panel sees it, the claimant had no subjective or objective fear in the first place.

propositions.text: Claimant's late Canadian refugee claim after alleged 2008 torture detracts from credibility and truthfulness.
propositions.quote: The claimant chose to come to Canada and make a refugee claim on November 15, 2010 as a mere after-thought...detracts from the claimant's credibility and truthfulness of the claim as so alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant lacked fear and that his late Canadian claim detracts from credibility.

propositions.text: Matos Quintana case states lack of credibility can justify disregarding documents and failure to claim asylum in US undermines credibility.
propositions.quote: Considering the obvious lack of credibility regarding the event at the centre of the claim...it was not unreasonable to not grant any probative value to all the documents submitted by the applicant...it was not unreasonable to determine that the fact that the applicant did not claim refugee status in the United States...could undermine his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The panel cites Matos Quintana case that failure to claim asylum in US undermines credibility and justifies disregarding documents.

propositions.text: Medical letter describes injuries consistent with police but doctor unaware of cause; court doubts claimant's truthfulness and injuries as alleged.
propositions.quote: the doctor has no idea that the injuries stem from police assaults...inspires little confidence that the claimant suffered problems and injuries as so alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The court doubts claimant's truthfulness and injuries despite medical letter describing injuries consistent with police.

propositions.text: Rokni and Danailov cases hold medical evidence cannot cure credibility deficiencies and opinion evidence depends on truth of facts.
propositions.quote: a psychiatric letter submitted as evidence...cannot possibly serve as a cure-all for any and all deficiencies in a claimant's testimony...opinion evidence is only as valid as the truth of the facts on which it is based.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites cases that medical evidence cannot fix credibility issues and depends on truth of facts.

propositions.text: Claimant's lawyer requested more time to provide original documents and additional evidence.
propositions.quote: it was requested for the panel to exercise its discretion and allow more time for the claimant to provide the original documents...and documents from SDP.

propositions.text: Panel refused more time as claimant had sufficient time since 2008 to gather evidence and meet onus.
propositions.quote: The panel advised that more time would not be given...There has been more than sufficient time for the claimant to have gathered all of his material...with a view of meeting his onus.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant requested more time for documents; panel refused due to sufficient prior time.

propositions.text: Panel considered post-hearing submissions including SDP letter which lacked evidence of risk to claimant's life and gave it little weight.
propositions.quote: the letter from SDP...contains little information that would suggest that the claimant's life was at risk...The panel gives little weight to the letter from SDP as so submitted.

propositions.text: If claimant's life was at risk, he would have claimed asylum in US and provided evidence to US authorities during 2.5 years there.
propositions.quote: If this was so the case, then it would be reasonable to expect that the claimant would have made a claim and provide the appropriate supporting documentary evidence to U.S. immigration authorities while he was in the United States for 2.5 years.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds SDP letter unpersuasive and notes claimant's failure to claim asylum in US undermines risk claim.

propositions.text: Membership application to Alevi Cultural Association does not prove membership or risk to claimant's life as an Alevi.
propositions.quote: This is a membership application and does not prove that the claimant is or was a member...Even if the claimant was, that does not indicate that...the claimant's life was or would be at risk

propositions.text: Panel gives little weight to the membership document.
propositions.quote: The panel again gives little weight to the document.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the Alevi membership document unpersuasive and gives it little weight.

propositions.text: Military document in evidence is not original and does not change panel's position; given little or no weight.
propositions.quote: it does not appear to be an original document...does not change the panel's position...The panel assigns little or no weight to this document.

paragraphs.summary: The panel assigns little or no weight to the military document, which is not original and does not affect findings.

propositions.text: There is little credible evidence to believe claimant's life is at risk or he would face persecution or torture if returned to Turkey.
propositions.quote: there is little or no credible evidence...that the claimant's life is at risk...no serious possibility or reasonable chance that the claimant would face persecution...no danger of torture should the claimant return to Turkey.

propositions.text: Panel has difficulty believing claimant's evidence and finds no risk of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment.
propositions.quote: the panel has difficulty believing the evidence as so submitted...would not suffer cruel or unusual treatment or punishment

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds no credible evidence of risk or persecution if claimant returns to Turkey and doubts claimant's evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant is not a Convention refugee and claim is rejected under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee...The panel rejects this claim pursuant to both sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes claimant is not a Convention refugee and rejects the claim under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
